---
title: "P1 — Building a functioning plant"
---

## The question

A seedling has no mouth, circulating blood or skeleton. Nevertheless, it must
obtain carbon, water and minerals, transport material between organs and support
itself against gravity. Its solution depends on how cells are connected and
specialised. Explain walls, vacuoles, plastids and three tissue systems;
distinguish division from expansion; and connect nuclear and organellar genomes
to cell function.

## Compartments make different processes possible

A plasma membrane surrounds each living cell and controls exchange. A
cellulose-containing wall lies outside it. The wall resists deformation and
helps connect cells, but it does not replace selective membrane transport.
Water and many small solutes can move through wall spaces; crossing a membrane
is a different step. Always distinguish the boundary being crossed.

The large central vacuole in many mature cells is surrounded by the tonoplast.
It stores solutes, contributes to pH regulation and degradation, and allows
a cell to enlarge without filling the entire volume with cytoplasm. Solute
accumulation can promote water entry. The resulting pressure against the wall,
**turgor**, supports non-woody tissues. A plant can wilt before its cells die:
reduced turgor changes organ mechanics.

Chloroplasts capture light energy and support carbon fixation. They are one
type of plastid; other plastids store starch or contain pigments. Many root
cells lack photosynthetically active chloroplasts. Mitochondria support
respiration in green cells as well as roots. Photosynthesis does not remove a
leaf's need for respiration. Different organelles contribute to the same cell.

## A resisting wall must also permit growth

Primary walls contain cellulose microfibrils within a matrix of other
polysaccharides and proteins. Their organisation influences the direction and
ease of expansion. Turgor supplies force, while controlled wall loosening
permits irreversible enlargement. Raising water pressure is not a complete
growth explanation: a stiff wall can resist it, and new membrane and wall
material must be supplied as a cell enlarges.

In an elongating root cell, water enters, the wall yields and length increases.
Reinforcing components help constrain expansion. Later, some specialised cells
deposit a secondary wall inside the primary wall. Lignified secondary walls
provide support and resist collapse in conducting xylem elements. Expanding
leaf cells and conducting tubes face different mechanical demands; their walls
are not interchangeable containers.

Neighbouring cells communicate through **plasmodesmata**, membrane-lined
connections through walls. Connected cytoplasm forms the **symplast**; walls
and extracellular spaces form the **apoplast**. These terms describe routes,
not separate organs. A solute moving through the apoplast can subsequently
cross a membrane and enter the symplast. This distinction becomes important
for [root uptake](../water-nutrition/index.qmd).

## Tissues connect cellular features to function

Roots and shoots contain organs such as leaves, stems and flowers. An organ
contains several tissues. Three systems provide a useful starting framework:

| Tissue system | Contributions | Structure–function example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dermal | Protection and exchange | Cuticle limits uncontrolled water loss; stomata permit adjustable gas exchange |
| Ground | Photosynthesis, storage and support | Mesophyll exposes photosynthetic cells to internal air spaces |
| Vascular | Transport and support | Xylem supplies water/minerals; phloem connects carbon sources and sinks |

Ground tissues include different cell types. Parenchyma often retains living
contents for metabolism or storage. Collenchyma supplies flexible support in
growing regions. Sclerenchyma commonly has strongly reinforced secondary walls.
Use names to predict observations: wall thickness, living contents, air spaces,
cell arrangement and position. One characteristic rarely identifies a specimen
unambiguously. Combine features and relationships with surrounding tissues.

A leaf illustrates coordination. CO2 enters an internal air space through a
stoma and reaches mesophyll. Light reaches chloroplasts. Water arrives through
xylem, and exported sugars leave through phloem. Opening stomata supports CO2
entry but also allows water vapour to escape. The arrangement links carbon
acquisition to water balance.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  air[Atmospheric CO2] --> pore[Stoma and air spaces]
  pore --> mes[Mesophyll chloroplasts]
  roots[Root water uptake] --> xy[Xylem]
  xy --> mes
  light[Light] --> mes
  mes --> sugars[Exported assimilate]
  sugars --> ph[Phloem]
  ph --> sink[Growing or storage tissues]
```

This original schematic shows functional connections; it is not an anatomical
section and does not imply that all transported carbon follows one route.

## Conducting tissues differ

Water-conducting tracheids and vessel elements are dead at functional maturity;
their reinforced walls remain. Living xylem parenchyma occurs alongside them,
so calling the whole tissue dead is inaccurate. In flowering plants,
sieve-tube elements remain living but lose their nuclei during maturation.
Companion cells support their function. Damage to living membranes can therefore
affect phloem differently from an intact water-filled xylem conduit.

Compare roots and leaves. Root hairs are extensions of epidermal cells that
increase contact with soil, not tiny roots. The endodermis helps control routes
into the root vascular region. Leaf mesophyll is arranged around light and gas
exchange. The organs share basic cell biology but emphasise different tasks.

## Meristems permit continuing organ production

An embryo establishes a body axis, but much of the mature plant develops after
germination. **Meristems** maintain populations of dividing cells. Root and
shoot apical meristems contribute to primary growth in length. Lateral
meristems support secondary thickening in plants that undergo it. Vascular
cambium produces secondary xylem inward and secondary phloem outward; cork
cambium contributes protective outer tissue. Grasses can retain basal growth
regions, allowing leaves to elongate after exposed tips are cut.

Cell production, expansion and differentiation are different processes. A root
can become longer through more cells, larger cells, or both. Regions near its
tip emphasise these processes differently, with transitions rather than
perfectly separated compartments. A short root does not automatically establish
slower division. Compare cell numbers, cell lengths and transition positions.

Differentiation changes gene expression and cellular organisation without
necessarily changing DNA sequence. Some mature cells can resume division under
suitable conditions, which matters in regeneration. However, regeneration
depends on genotype, developmental state and culture conditions. Every mature
cell is not guaranteed to produce a whole plant.

## Three genomes cooperate

Plant cells contain nuclear, plastid and mitochondrial genomes. Nuclear DNA
encodes most cellular proteins, including many that function inside the two
organelles. Such proteins are synthesised outside the organelle and imported.
Organellar genomes encode smaller sets of essential products. Function depends
on coordination across compartments rather than three self-sufficient systems.

A gene is a DNA region whose expression contributes a functional RNA or protein.
Changing expression can alter a process without changing sequence. Leaf and
root cells can share a nuclear genome while using different gene sets.
Tissue-specific expression later helps explain development and biotechnology.
Organellar inheritance is often uniparental, but patterns vary among species;
do not assume a universal maternal rule.

## Make a testable prediction

A plant with intact green leaves but reduced root hairs may struggle to obtain
resources in some soils. Other root properties could compensate. Reduced hairs
alone do not establish which transporter or hormone changed. Explain the chain:
structure → exchange opportunity → resource availability → whole-plant effect.
